q-49554:
Note that we can rewrite this integral as

$$
\int \frac{\text{d}x}{3|x|\sqrt{9{x}^{2}-1}}=\int \frac{\text{d}x}{|3x|\sqrt{(3x)^{2}-1}}.
$$

This integral now resembles the basic one for $\text{arcsec},$

$$
\int \frac{1}{|u|\sqrt{{u}^{2}-1}}\text{d}u=\text{arcsec}(u)+C.
$$

The only difference is that instead of $u$ as the variable, we have $3x.$

So, let's substitute $u=3x.$ Differentiating, we get

$$
\frac{\text{d}u}{\text{d}x}=3\,⟹\,\text{d}x=\frac{1}{3}\text{d}u.
$$

Using the above, we can write the integral in terms of $u$ and evaluate:

$$
\begin{aligned}\begin{aligned}\int \frac{1}{3|x|\sqrt{9{x}^{2}-1}}\,\text{d}x & =\int \frac{1}{|3x|\sqrt{(3x)^{2}-1}}\,\text{d}x \\  & =\int \frac{1}{|u|\sqrt{{u}^{2}-1}}\cdot (\frac{1}{3}\text{d}u) \\  & =\frac{1}{3}\int \frac{\text{d}u}{|u|\sqrt{{u}^{2}-1}} \\  & =\frac{1}{3}\text{arcsec }u+C \\  & =\frac{\text{arcsec}(3x)}{3}+C\end{aligned}\end{aligned}
$$

q-114054:
Note that we can rewrite this integral as

$$
\int \frac{\text{d}x}{|x|\sqrt{6{x}^{2}-1}}=\int \frac{\sqrt{6}}{|\sqrt{6}x|\sqrt{(\sqrt{6}x)^{2}-1}}\text{d}x.
$$

This integral now resembles the basic one for $\text{arcsec},$

$$
\int \frac{1}{|u|\sqrt{{u}^{2}-1}}\text{d}u=\text{arcsec}(u)+C.
$$

The only difference is that instead of $u$ as the variable, we have $\sqrt{6}x.$

So, let's substitute $u=\sqrt{6}x.$ Differentiating, we get

$$
\frac{\text{d}u}{\text{d}x}=\sqrt{6}\,⟹\,\text{d}x=\frac{1}{\sqrt{6}}\text{d}u.
$$

Using the above, we can write the integral in terms of $u$ and evaluate:

$$
\begin{aligned}\begin{aligned}\int \frac{1}{|x|\sqrt{6{x}^{2}-1}}\,\text{d}x & =\int \frac{\sqrt{6}}{|\sqrt{6}x|\sqrt{(\sqrt{6}x)^{2}-1}}\,\text{d}x \\  & =\sqrt{6}\int \frac{1}{|u|\sqrt{{u}^{2}-1}}\cdot (\frac{1}{\sqrt{6}}\text{d}u) \\  & =\sqrt{6}\cdot \frac{1}{\sqrt{6}}\int \frac{\text{d}u}{|u|\sqrt{{u}^{2}-1}} \\  & =\text{arcsec }u+C \\  & =\text{arcsec}(\sqrt{6}x)+C\end{aligned}\end{aligned}
$$

q-181779:
The Cartesian product $A\times B$ consists of all ordered pairs whose first coordinate belongs to $A$ and whose second coordinate belongs to $B.$

$$
A\times B={(a,b)\,:\,a\in A,\,b\in B}
$$

In this case, the set 

$$
S=N\times R
$$

 
contains every point in ${R}^{2}$ whose $x$-coordinate is a natural number and whose $y$-coordinate is any real number.

$$
S={(x,y)\,:\,x\in N,\,y\in R}
$$

To visualize $S,$ consider ${S}_{1}⊂S$ containing all points whose $x$-coordinate equals $1$ and whose $y$-coordinate is any real number.

$$
{S}_{1}={(1,y)\,:\,y\in R}
$$

We can represent ${S}_{1}$ in the plane as follows:

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/question-capture/14094658/assets/067b3b386273b09d5614f934f6525bd3e43ff46f420eb8aa7e744f635ff6d101.png)

Next, consider ${S}_{2}⊂S$ containing all points whose $x$-coordinate equals $2$ and whose $y$-coordinate is any real number.

$$
{S}_{2}={(2,y)\,:\,y\in R}.
$$

We can represent ${S}_{2}$ in the plane as follows:

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/question-capture/14094658/assets/a870f65350ad00d258471079a34bec49a47d331c176dc7a91b3c7aae5ae968dd.png)

We can create the subsets ${S}_{3},{S}_{4},{S}_{5},…$ similarly. Our Cartesian product consists of the *union* of these subsets:

$$
\begin{aligned}R\times N & ={S}_{1}\cup {S}_{2}\cup {S}_{3}\cup … \\  & ={⋃}_{i\in N}{S}_{i}\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, we can visualize $R\times N$ as the set of vertical lines shown in the diagram below.

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/question-capture/14094658/assets/c0df23ec47d729f597c02acff1530dd646a6f6c506a6497a8cb4d75b7fce5e74.png)

q-181985:
The Cartesian product $A\times B$ consists of all ordered pairs whose first coordinate belongs to $A$ and whose second coordinate belongs to $B.$

$$
A\times B={(a,b)\,:\,a\in A,\,b\in B}
$$

In this case, the set

$$
S=[-1,0]\times [-1,1]
$$

contains every point in ${R}^{2}$ whose $x$-coordinate is any real number in the interval $[-1,0]$ and whose $y$-coordinate is any real number in the interval $[-1,1].$

$$
S={(x,y)\,:\,x\in [-1,0],\,y\in [-1,1]}.
$$

To visualize $S$, consider ${S}_{0}⊂S$ containing all points whose $x$-coordinate equals $0$ and whose $y$-coordinate is any real number in the interval $[-1,1].$

$$
{S}_{0}={(0,y)\,:\,y\in [-1,1]}
$$

We can represent ${S}_{0}$ in the plane as follows:

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/question-capture/14094658/assets/c93f3ad399b88ccbaac990f8f73e93cfdcb1192f52b9b12f2d3ce178776fa13b.png)

Now, consider a general ${S}_{i}⊂S$ containing all points whose $x$-coordinate equals some $i\in [-1,0]$ and whose $y$-coordinate is any real number in the interval $[-1,1].$

$$
{S}_{i}={(i,y)\,:\,y\in [-1,1]}
$$

For each $i\in [-1,0],$ ${S}_{i}$ is a vertical line segment from the point $(i,-1)$ to the point $(i,1).$

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/question-capture/14094658/assets/6557201d202a401a92ee37c9a69eab9ab6ab87c6342dbb9d2afebae30141346f.png)

Our Cartesian product $S$ is the union of these subsets over $I=[-1,0]:$

$$
S={⋃}_{i\in I}{S}_{i}.
$$

As $i$ runs over $I,$ these line segments sweep the following rectangle that represents the union ${⋃}_{i\in I}{S}_{i}:$

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/question-capture/14094658/assets/97a74b119ddb8a618d6564bc077d03a5a4ceb7152702beb3682f2eab1a436b70.png)

q-65017:
Suppose we have a second-order inhomogeneous ODE given in the form

$$
a(x){y}^{″}+b(x){y}^{′}+c(x)y=f(x).
$$

The associated homogeneous equation is constructed by replacing $f(x)$ with zero:

$$
a(x){y}^{″}+b(x){y}^{′}+c(x)y=0
$$

Therefore, in our case, the associated homogeneous equation is

$$
{x}^{2}{y}^{″}-{y}^{′}+3y=0.
$$

q-93952:
If a second-order differential equation for the function $y(x)$ is given with two conditions specified at the *same* location in the domain of $y,$ then this is an **initial value problem**.

Let's go through each equation in turn.

- The first system is not an initial value problem. It contains an equation only. No conditions are specified.

- The second system is not an initial value problem. It consists of a differential equation together with two conditions at different points in the domain of $y(x)$ (i.e., at $x=1$ and $x=2$). This is a **boundary value problem.**

- The third system is an initial value problem. The differential equation is together with two conditions at the same location in the domain of $y(x)$ (i.e., at $x=1$).

q-74600:
By definition, $u\in Π$ if there exist $t$ and $s$ such that

$$
\begin{aligned}sb+tc & =u \\ s[\begin{aligned}-1 \\ 4 \\ -5\end{aligned}]+t[\begin{aligned}3 \\ -9 \\ 15\end{aligned}] & =[\begin{aligned}2 \\ -2 \\ 11\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$

So, we have the following system of equations:

$$
{\begin{aligned}-s+3t=2 \\ 4s-9t=-2 \\ -5s+15t=11\end{aligned}
$$

To solve the system above, we set up and row reduce an augmented matrix:

$$
\begin{aligned} & [\begin{aligned}-1 & 3 & 2 \\ 4 & -9 & -2 \\ -5 & 15 & 11\end{aligned}] & {R}_{2} & :={R}_{2}+4{R}_{1} \\  & ∼[\begin{aligned}-1 & 3 & 2 \\ 0 & 3 & 6 \\ -5 & 15 & 11\end{aligned}] & {R}_{3} & :={R}_{3}-5{R}_{1} \\  & ∼[\begin{aligned}-1 & 3 & 2 \\ 0 & 3 & 6 \\ 0 & 0 & 1\end{aligned}]\end{aligned}
$$

The third row of the augmented matrix now corresponds to the equation $0{x}_{1}+0{x}_{2}=1,$ which has no solution.

So, there are no values of $s$ and $t$ such that 

$$
\begin{aligned}sb+tc=u.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, we conclude that $u$ does *not* lie on the plane $Π.$

q-74607:
By definition, $u\in Π$ if there exist $t$ and $s$ such that

$$
\begin{aligned}sb+tc & =u \\ s[\begin{aligned}1 \\ 2 \\ 3\end{aligned}]+t[\begin{aligned}3 \\ 8 \\ -7\end{aligned}] & =[\begin{aligned}9 \\ 22 \\ -5\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$

So, we have the following system of equations:

$$
{\begin{aligned}s+3t=9 \\ 2s+8t=22 \\ 3s-7t=-5\end{aligned}
$$

To solve the system above, we set up and row reduce an augmented matrix:

$$
\begin{aligned} & [\begin{aligned}1 & 3 & 9 \\ 2 & 8 & 22 \\ 3 & -7 & -5\end{aligned}] & {R}_{2} & :={R}_{2}-2{R}_{1} \\  & ∼[\begin{aligned}1 & 3 & 9 \\ 0 & 2 & 4 \\ 3 & -7 & -5\end{aligned}] & {R}_{3} & :={R}_{3}-3{R}_{1} \\  & ∼[\begin{aligned}1 & 3 & 9 \\ 0 & 2 & 4 \\ 0 & -16 & -32\end{aligned}] & {R}_{3} & :={R}_{3}+8{R}_{2} \\  & ∼[\begin{aligned}1 & 3 & 9 \\ 0 & 2 & 4 \\ 0 & 0 & 0\end{aligned}]\end{aligned}
$$

Now, we have the system

$$
{\begin{aligned}s+3t=9 \\ 2t=4 \\ 0=0.\end{aligned}
$$

From the second equation, we get

$$
2t=4\,⟹\,t=2.
$$

Substituting into the first equation, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}s+3t & =9 \\ s+3(2) & =9 \\ s & =3.\end{aligned}
$$

Since we found a solution $s=3,\,t=2,$ we conclude that $u$ does indeed lie on the plane $Π.$ In fact, we have

$$
u=3b+2c.
$$

Finally, $s\cdot t=3\cdot 2=6.$

q-109886:
If $X$ is a discrete random variable with probability mass function $f(x)$ and sample space $S,$ the expected value of ${X}^{2}$ is given by

$$
\text{E}[{X}^{2}]={\sum }_{x\in S}{x}^{2}\cdot f(x).
$$

Summing up the products of each squared value of $X$ and its associated probability, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\text{E}[{X}^{2}] & ={\sum }_{x\in S}{x}^{2}\cdot f(x) \\  & ={0}^{2}\cdot 0.05+{1}^{2}\cdot 0.4+{2}^{2}\cdot 0.1+{3}^{2}\cdot 0.25+{4}^{2}\cdot 0.2 \\  & =0\cdot 0.05+1\cdot 0.4+4\cdot 0.1+9\cdot 0.25+16\cdot 0.2 \\  & =6.25.\end{aligned}
$$

q-126776:
If $X$ is a discrete random variable with probability mass function $f(x)$ and sample space $S,$ the expected value of ${X}^{2}$ is given by

$$
\text{E}[{X}^{2}]={\sum }_{x\in S}{x}^{2}\cdot f(x).
$$

Summing up the products of each squared value of $X$ and its associated probability, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\text{E}[{X}^{2}] & ={\sum }_{x\in S}{x}^{2}\cdot f(x) \\  & ={10}^{2}\cdot 0.25+{20}^{2}\cdot 0.4+{30}^{2}\cdot 0.35 \\  & =100\cdot 0.25+400\cdot 0.4+900\cdot 0.35 \\  & =500.\end{aligned}
$$
